6.8 The Stock Research Process (Brief)

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

All lessons, questions and reference answers on this site were generated by AI and have not been reviewed by a professional. Their correctness is not guaranteed. If you find an error, please report it with the link at the bottom of the page. The content is for learning only and is not investment advice.

Earlier lessons showed that for most households low-cost index funds are the core of the portfolio (6.3 Active vs. Passive Investing). This lesson briefly introduces the process of researching a single stock: even without picking stocks, these methods help in understanding the companies one owns, judging other people’s recommendations, and writing the stock report in the capstone project.

Reading company filings

Section titled “Reading company filings”

All filings of US listed companies are freely available on the SEC’s EDGAR system:

  • The Form 10-K is the audited annual report, filed by large companies within 60 days of the fiscal year end. The parts most worth reading are: the business description (how the company makes money, its segments and customers), risk factors, management’s discussion and analysis (MD&A, which explains why results changed), and the financial statements and notes (3.7 Financial Statement Analysis).
  • The 10-Q is the quarterly report: unaudited, similar to the 10-K but shorter.
  • The 8-K is filed within 4 business days of a major event (mergers, management changes, earnings releases and so on).
  • The proxy statement (DEF 14A) shows the structure and targets of executive pay and the makeup of the board.
  • On the earnings call, management presents results and answers analysts’ questions, often giving guidance for the next quarter or year.
Check C1
The guidance for next year that management gives on the earnings call is audited, so it is more reliable than the historical figures in the 10-K.
What do auditors audit, results that have happened or forecasts? What motives might management have when giving guidance?

Industry analysis

Section titled “Industry analysis”

A company’s long-run profitability depends heavily on its industry. Porter’s (1979) five forces analyze how much of an industry’s profit stays with the companies in it: the intensity of rivalry among existing firms; the threat of new entrants (barriers to entry); the threat of substitutes; the bargaining power of suppliers; and the bargaining power of buyers. The weaker the five forces, the higher the industry’s average profits.

Within an industry, whether a company can earn more than its cost of capital for a long time depends on whether it has a moat (economic moat): network effects, switching costs, economies of scale, brands or patents. The measure is the gap between return on invested capital (return on invested capital) and the weighted average cost of capital (weighted average cost of capital), and how long that gap can last (Exercises Question 3).

Check C2
US airline passenger numbers have grown over the long run, yet the industry's long-run average profit margin is very low, with several large airlines going bankrupt. By the five forces, the main reason is:
The question says passenger numbers have grown. Does large demand guarantee high profits? Who takes the profit?
If the whole industry has been like this for decades, is it more likely a matter of individual ability or of industry structure?

Valuation: running the DCF in reverse

Section titled “Valuation: running the DCF in reverse”

DCF (3.10 Equity Valuation II: Discounted Free Cash Flow) and relative valuation (3.11 Equity Valuation III: Relative Valuation) both depend on assumptions about the future, and the results are very sensitive to growth and discount rates. A practical approach turns the question around: instead of estimating what the company is worth, ask “what growth does today’s price imply the market expects?”; this is a reverse DCF. Then judge whether that growth is reasonable: compare it with the company’s history, the size of its industry and the past experience of similar companies.

Check C3
In Figure 3-1, raise the discount rate from 9% to 11%. For the same multiple (say 40), what happens to the implied growth, and why?
With a higher discount rate, what are the same future cash flows worth today? For the value still to equal the price, what must growth do?
Look at the curve and the readout: after changing the discount rate, does the growth at a multiple of 40 change?

The thesis and the case against it

Section titled “The thesis and the case against it”

The result of research should be written up as an investment thesis: why the price is below value now, how one’s view differs from the market consensus, what events might make the market see it, and what evidence would prove one wrong.

Just as important is writing out the case against seriously: what are the strongest reasons to be bearish? One can do a “pre-mortem”: suppose that three years from now this investment has lost 50%; what is the most likely reason? The aim is to counter confirmation bias and overconfidence (overconfidence): people tend to look for information that supports their views.

Finally there is position size. Even after thorough research, a single stock’s idiosyncratic risk is large (4.5 The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta), and the judgment of value may be wrong. A common practice is to limit any one stock’s share of the portfolio, keeping individual stocks as a small part outside the index core.

Check C4
A company has a wide moat, excellent management and steady growth, so its stock must be a good investment.
Does a stock's return depend on how the company performs, or on how it performs relative to the expectations built into the price paid? Do other investors know the company is good?
Check C5
Writing down before buying "what evidence would prove me wrong" mainly serves to:
Can writing down when one would be wrong change the stock price? Whose behavior does it change?
Think about how people often react after buying when the price falls and bad news appears (4.8 Behavioral Finance).

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • 10-Ks, 10-Qs, 8-Ks, proxy statements and earnings calls are the basic sources for researching a company; the 10-K is audited.
  • The five forces analyze how much of an industry’s profit companies keep; a moat decides whether ROIC can stay above WACC for long.
  • A reverse DCF finds the growth implied by the price, which can then be judged for reasonableness.
  • An investment thesis should state how one differs from the market and what evidence would prove one wrong; write the case against seriously; limit the size of single-stock positions.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
A software company has free cash flow of 4 dollars per share this year, and its stock is at 200 dollars. Use a discount rate of 9.5%, with free cash flow growing 3% a year forever after 10 years.
(a) Use a reverse DCF to find the yearly growth in free cash flow over the next 10 years implied by the price (code or a calculator may be used to solve).
(b) An analyst says: "This company's free cash flow grew 20% a year over the past 5 years; it is a great company, and buying now is sure to make money." Evaluate this statement. Against what would you judge whether the implied growth is reasonable?
Question 2
A company reports record annual profit. From its 10-K: revenue rose 10%, from 1 billion to 1.1 billion dollars; year-end receivables rose 40%, from 164.4 million to 230.2 million dollars; operating cash flow fell from the year before.
(a) Compute days sales outstanding for each year (year-end receivables / revenue × 365).
(b) The press release says "record results and strong growth". Evaluate this statement: what might these figures indicate? Which parts of the 10-K would you check further?

Question 4
An investor used to hold 100% in a stock index fund (volatility 16%). After months of researching a company, he decides to move 30% of the portfolio into its stock. The stock's volatility is 40%, and its correlation with the index is 0.5.
(a) Roughly what is the portfolio's volatility after the change?
(b) He says: "I've researched this company thoroughly, so this investment is much less risky than buying a stock I don't understand." Evaluate this statement and give advice.
